note: Existing-source, strict-license-screened public gallery. Additional historical photos remain held from this site. Anatomy overlays are teaching annotations, not a separate verified voucher determination.

tiles.heading: 01 · LOOK HERE FIRST — AIRY TUMBLING PANICLE
tiles.details: Actual full flowering architecture appears in D. cognata panels 2 and 4 (indices 1,3), with individual terminal spikelets in panels 6–7 (indices 5,6). The airy panicle is visible but alone cannot confirm a Hays County voucher or microscopic glume lengths.
tiles.short: A wide, open, wiry broom with separate oval spikelets on fine stalks.

tiles.heading: 02 · KNOTTY PERENNIAL BASE AND TRUE LIGULE
tiles.details: Panels 1–2 (indices 0–1) now show a source-identified collected whole plant with attached fibrous roots, leafy basal tillers and wiry flowering culm. At the leaf blade–sheath junction, however, the true free inner membrane has NOT been exposed and measured; a sheath surface is not the ligule. Panel 3 (index 2) shows a pale uneven blade edge, not a measured same-leaf two-margin comparison. Some regional sources differ on auricle-like lobes; don't decide from these alone.
tiles.short: Perennial leafy crown; membranous ligule ~0.2–1.5 mm (often ~0.5 mm in Texas key).
tiles.status: ROOTED BASE SHOWN — TRUE LIGULE PHOTO MISSING

tiles.heading: 03 · MEASURE THE MATURE SPIKELET
tiles.details: D. cognata terminal spikelets are visibly spaced along hair-thin pedicels in panels 6–7 (indices 5–6). With no scale they cannot establish exact dimensions or separate glumes and lemmas. Collect 3–5 ripe spikelets from a botanically authenticated specimen and photograph with 1-mm reference; published range is about 2.2–3.1 mm.
tiles.short: Oval spikelets ~2.2–3.1 mm; solitary on slender pedicels.

tiles.heading: 04 · TWO GLUMES, TWO DIFFERENT FLORETS
tiles.details: A mature spikelet has a reduced lower glume, a much longer upper glume, one lower sterile floret with an approximately 7-veined lemma, and one upper fertile floret with lemma and palea. No long glume or lemma awns. Minnesota Wildflowers describes the upper glume as sometimes finely hairy between veins. Do not confuse the two FLORETS with two separate spikelets or label microscopic bracts in unresolvable gallery pixels.
tiles.short: Tiny lower glume ≤1 mm; upper glume ~1.8–2.8 mm, usually 3–5-veined.

tiles.heading: 05 · LOOK-ALIKES AND HAIR PLACEMENT
tiles.details: D. ciliaris in the final three gallery panels 8–10 (indices 7–9) shows compact, one-sided fingerlike racemes and overlapping spikelets, unlike the dispersed units of D. cognata. Compare Panicum capillare (hair-fringe ligule, usually annual) and Eragrostis spectabilis (multifloret spikelets) from sources, not from these D. ciliaris images. Actual D. cognata swollen hairy branch axils and open inner ligule remain photographic gaps.
tiles.short: Not crabgrass fingers, not Panicum's annual habit, not lovegrass multiflowered spikelets.

tiles.heading: 06 · PUBLIC-READY GATE
tiles.details: CURRENT PHOTO EVIDENCE: seven physically archived D. cognata photographs in indices 0–6 show a dug-up connected fibrous-rooted crown and flowering culm (0–1), candidate pale uneven blade margin (2), airy panicle (3), basal tuft (4), and individual terminal spikelets (5–6). Three D. ciliaris look-alike panels occupy indices 7–9. These are 18 existing gross markers on the species and 8 on the different-species comparisons, NOT evidence of a measured ligule, hairy branch axil or dissected glumes. NEEDS_PUBLIC_PHOTO: opened ~0.2–1.5 mm true membranous ligule with 1-mm scale; swollen hairy flowering branch axil; opposing margins of same leaf; calibrated mature spikelets and glume/lemma/palea dissection; Hays-area in-situ rooted habitat specimen. NEEDS_SITE_QA: verify exact CC BY/CC0 credits, panel indices, arrows and rights-filtered mobile Pages deployment. Preserve Hays BONAP county-native hold.
tiles.short: FIELD_READY_PHOTO_GAPS — don't certify county native status or microscopic completion.
tiles.status: FIELD_READY_PHOTO_GAPS — TRUE LIGULE AND MACRO ANATOMY NOT PHOTOGRAPHED

steps.title: 1 · First, recognize the plant
steps.look_for: FALL WITCHGRASS (formerly Leptoloma cognatum): look for an extremely OPEN, diffuse broomlike panicle on hair-fine wiry stems with solitary small oval spikelets near branch ends. Three real source photographs now show the head, basal leafy tuft, and isolated terminal spikelets. The characteristic swollen pubescent branch junctions and pale crinkled blade margin still need actual macro pictures; don't draw these hairs on unresolvable pixels. Native to Texas at STATE scale, but Hays BONAP county status remains unchanged/unverified.
steps.why_it_matters: Start with the recorded recognition characters before making a species identification.

steps.title: 2 · Examine the whole plant
steps.look_for: START panels 1–2 (indices 0–1): original source-labelled Texas plants have a photographed perennial-looking rooted basal crown physically attached to narrow leaves and at least one wiry flowering head. Real attached fibrous roots are not guessed from soil shadows.
steps.why_it_matters: Habit and growing context are supporting evidence, not proof of hidden roots or rhizomes.

steps.title: 3 · Inspect leaves, collar and nodes
steps.look_for: Panels 1–2 (indices 0–1) now show a source-identified collected whole plant with attached fibrous roots, leafy basal tillers and wiry flowering culm. At the leaf blade–sheath junction, however, the true free inner membrane has NOT been exposed and measured; a sheath surface is not the ligule. Panel 3 (index 2) shows a pale uneven blade edge, not a measured same-leaf two-margin comparison. Some regional sources differ on auricle-like lobes; don't decide from these alone.
steps.why_it_matters: Examine the real structures; the photo may not expose or measure all the described characters.

steps.title: 4 · Check the flowering structure
steps.look_for: Actual full flowering architecture appears in D. cognata panels 2 and 4 (indices 1,3), with individual terminal spikelets in panels 6–7 (indices 5,6). The airy panicle is visible but alone cannot confirm a Hays County voucher or microscopic glume lengths.
steps.why_it_matters: Use an attached, correctly identified specimen when deciding the flower or spikelet structures.

steps.title: 5 · Compare similar grasses
steps.look_for: Against D. ciliaris, there are NO fingerlike tightly paired spikelet racemes: the source photos show widely separated individually stalked units in a fragile branching broom. Other airy genera such as Panicum, Sporobolus and some Eragrostis can look similar; inspect the oval spikelet and actual leaf margin and hairy axillary swellings. Aristida has conspicuous three-parted true awns, absent on D. cognata. Its older Leptoloma cognatum name is a synonym, not a second card.
steps.why_it_matters: Confirm at least two independent botanical characters; do not remove a native candidate from color alone.

panels.label: Fall witchgrass — basal tuft and upright wirelike culms
panels.caption: Shaun Pogacnik's Pennsylvania source-labelled late-season plant shows a low leafy tuft with narrow dry blades and several fine flowering stems. Image does not prove a woody or perennial underground base, or the diagnostic wavy leaf margin at scale.
panels.creator: Shaun Pogacnik
panels.annotation_note: Hays Botany displays overlaid numbered anatomy pointers; the source JPEG itself is unchanged.

panels.label: Fall witchgrass — isolated oval spikelets on threadlike stalks
panels.caption: Shaun Pogacnik's Pennsylvania macro shows elongated tiny pale oval spikelets individually situated on long, very slender purplish branch tips. This is useful opposite tightly packed crabgrass racemes. No exact spikelet length, hairy branch axil or lemma anatomy is measurable here.
panels.creator: Shaun Pogacnik
panels.annotation_note: Hays Botany displays overlaid numbered anatomy pointers; the source JPEG itself is unchanged.

panels.label: Fall witchgrass — physically archived terminal spikelets and hair-fine reddish branches
panels.caption: Shaun Pogacnik's Pennsylvania photograph shows individual pale oval spikelets widely spaced on reddish, hair-thin flowering stalks. Follow a stalk to its terminal spikelet; compare this airy architecture against southern crabgrass's tightly packed, one-sided racemes. No millimeter ruler is present, so do not infer glume, lemma, ligule or branch-axil hair measurements.
panels.creator: Shaun Pogacnik
panels.annotation_note: Hays Botany displays overlaid numbered anatomy pointers; the source JPEG itself is unchanged.

memory_rule: CILIARIS = FINGERLIKE ONE-SIDED RACEMES AND CROWDED SPIKELETS. COGNATA = AIRY BRANCHES AND DISTANT TERMINAL SPIKELETS.
safety_note: 11 source species photographs physically in GitHub; 12 field teaching panels (9 actual species panels +3 unmistakably other-taxon southern crabgrass look-alikes); four new anatomy gross pointers. Conservative photographic six-role=5/6=83%: roots, habit, real separate spikelets and lookalike contrast established, but free inner ligule, glume/lemma microdissection and hairy branch-axil macro still missing. No Hays county native reclassification.
field_rule: First find the true extremely OPEN branching panicle (unlike Digitaria ciliaris fingerlike racemes), verify an actually connected rooted base and flowering culm, then inspect the INNER ~0.5-mm erose membranous ligule. The pictured split OUTER sheath edge is not enough.
photo_data_caution: Missing or restricted comparison photographs have not been replaced by guesses. Source statements are not proof the associated structure is visible in any available photo.
